title: Leadership Styles
essentialQuestion: Is there an ideal leadership style, or only a suitable style for a particular situation?
speakingGoal: Evaluate leadership approaches, qualify claims, and recommend a style based on context.

warmup.instructions: 1. What leadership style brings out your best work?

prompts.question: Can the same leadership style succeed with one team and fail with another?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: Yes; situational leadership requires adapting style based on team maturity, domain ambiguity, and organizational context.
No; one rigid leadership style works identically across all teams and industries.
Leadership style has zero correlation with team performance.

prompts.explanation: A high-direction style that steadies an inexperienced squad will frustrate a senior team of specialists. Great leaders diagnose context and adapt dynamically.

prompts.question: When does executive decisiveness cross the line into destructive control?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: When leaders stop listening to dissenting evidence, micromanage execution, and punish feedback.
Whenever a leader makes a firm decision following consultation.
Decisiveness can never have negative consequences in business.

prompts.explanation: Decisiveness provides momentum; authoritarian control stifles innovation. Leaders must remain firm on strategic destination while empowering teams on execution.

mainInput.title: 2. Main Input - The Leader Who Changed Her Approach
mainInput.context: When Elena became head of a fast-growing design team, she tried to lead the same way she had led a smaller operational group. She set detailed procedures, reviewed most decisions herself, and expected regular progress reports.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The approach initially created order, but experienced designers soon complained that it slowed them down. They wanted clearer goals and more freedom over how to reach them.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Elena could have concluded that the team was resistant to management. Instead, she reconsidered the situation. New employees still needed structure, while senior specialists needed autonomy.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: She changed her approach. Project goals, deadlines, and quality standards remained explicit, but experienced team members had greater control over methods. Junior employees received more frequent coaching. In urgent situations, Elena became more directive again.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Performance improved, but the more important lesson was not that one style was superior. It was that leadership effectiveness depended partly on task, experience, urgency, and the level of trust within the team.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: A highly participative style may work well when expertise is distributed across a group, yet it can be inefficient in a crisis. A directive approach may produce speed, but if used constantly it can reduce initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The question therefore shifts from "What is the best leadership style?" to "What does this situation require, and what might this approach cost?"

title: Organisational Change
essentialQuestion: Why do people resist change even when the business case appears strong?
speakingGoal: Explain the rationale for change, acknowledge losses and uncertainty, and build a credible implementation narrative.

warmup.instructions: 1. What kinds of change create the most resistance?

prompts.question: Is employee resistance to organizational change usually irrational?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: No; resistance is typically a rational response to loss of autonomy, unfamiliarity, or poorly communicated rationale.
Yes; employees resist purely out of spite for the company.
Change resistance only occurs when salaries are doubled.

prompts.explanation: People do not resist change; they resist being changed without consultation. Understanding their legitimate concerns is the first step toward effective change management.

prompts.question: What critical information do employees need before they will genuinely support change?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: The compelling 'why', how it affects their daily role, what training will be provided, and what success looks like.
Just a top-down mandate stating that compliance is mandatory by Monday.
Zero information so that the change remains an exciting surprise.

prompts.explanation: Change fails without emotional buy-in. Leaders must over-communicate the purpose behind the transition and provide tangible scaffolding and training.

mainInput.title: 2. Main Input - The Change Message That Failed
mainInput.context: A manufacturing company announces that it will replace several local planning systems with one shared platform.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The executive announcement emphasises efficiency: fewer duplicate systems, faster reporting, lower maintenance cost. Leaders expect employees to welcome the improvement.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Instead, resistance grows.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Local teams are not only worried about learning new software. Some fear losing control over processes they designed themselves. Others believe the central system may not reflect regional needs. A few supervisors worry that the new visibility will expose weak performance.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The implementation team changes its communication. Rather than repeating the efficiency argument, it begins to acknowledge what different groups may lose: familiar routines, local flexibility, status, and certainty.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Leaders also separate what is fixed from what is still open to influence. The company will use one shared platform, but teams can help design workflows, migration priorities, and training.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Resistance does not disappear, but the conversation becomes more productive.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The lesson is that a technically logical change can still create social and professional costs. People often ask two questions at the same time: "Will this help the organisation?" and "What will this mean for me?"

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: A credible change message needs to address both.

title: Cross Cultural Communication
essentialQuestion: How can professionals discuss cultural differences without turning them into stereotypes?
speakingGoal: Interpret behaviour cautiously, test assumptions, and adapt communication across different professional norms.

warmup.instructions: 1. Which workplace behaviours are interpreted differently across cultures?

prompts.question: Can broad cultural guidebooks sometimes inadvertently increase stereotyping?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: Yes; applying broad national generalizations can blind professionals to individual nuances, corporate culture, and personal styles.
No; every person from a given country behaves in 100% identical ways.
Culture plays zero role in international business negotiations.

prompts.explanation: Cultural frameworks provide helpful archetypes (e.g. high-context vs low-context), but they must be applied with humility and openness to individual variation.

prompts.question: How should you respond when an international colleague's behavior feels abrupt or rude?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

options.text: Pause and assume positive intent: consider whether direct communication norms or language differences explain the delivery.
Report them to international tribunals for breach of etiquette.

prompts.explanation: In cross-cultural work, attribute misunderstandings to communication conventions before malicious intent. Direct cultures value brevity; indirect cultures value diplomatic phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator

prompts.question: Why is having a logically superior idea rarely enough to gain cross-functional cooperation?

prompts.explanation: Lateral influence requires finding the 'WIIFM' (What's In It For Me) for the other department. Align your proposal with their core quarterly OKRs to secure genuine commitment.

prompts.question: When trying to build a coalition for a new initiative, who is strategically easiest to influence first?
prompts.hint: Choose the most effective workplace approach.

prompts.explanation: Do not waste initial momentum trying to convert hardened cynics. Build social proof and momentum with curious fence-sitters and early adopters first.

mainInput.title: 2. Main Input - The Project Nobody Owned
mainInput.context: Nabil is asked to lead a company-wide sustainability initiative. The difficulty is that none of the people whose cooperation he needs report to him.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Facilities controls energy use. Procurement chooses suppliers. Finance controls budgets. HR manages employee communication. Each department already has its own priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Nabil's first message is broad: "We all need to support sustainability." It receives polite agreement but little action.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: He then meets stakeholders individually. Facilities wants lower operating costs. Procurement is worried about supplier complexity. Finance wants measurable returns. HR wants an initiative employees can understand and participate in.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Nabil reframes the programme differently for each group while keeping the overall goal consistent. With Facilities, he discusses energy savings. With Finance, he proposes two projects with measurable payback periods. With Procurement, he starts with suppliers they already use.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: He also finds two respected managers willing to sponsor the initiative publicly.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Within three months, the programme has momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Nabil has no new formal power. What changes is the network around the idea: stakeholders can see their own interests in it, credible supporters are visible, and the first request is limited enough to feel manageable.

mainInput.title: ## 2. Main Input
mainInput.context:
### Sales Are Down—but Why?

A regional manager presents a chart showing that monthly sales fell by 12% in the northern region. Her first conclusion is immediate: “Our new pricing strategy is failing.”

An analyst asks to look more closely.

The decline began two weeks before the pricing change. One major distributor also reduced orders because it was moving warehouses. Meanwhile, sales of premium products actually increased, while lower-priced bulk orders fell sharply.

The team separates three layers.

**Observation:** total regional sales are 12% lower.

**Interpretation:** the decline may be partly connected to distributor disruption and product mix.

**Recommendation:** do not reverse the pricing strategy yet; track another month and analyse customers separately.

The analyst also points out that the available data cannot fully isolate cause and effect.

The final presentation changes from “Pricing caused a 12% decline” to “Sales fell 12%, but current evidence does not establish pricing as the main cause.”

The second statement sounds less dramatic, but it is more useful. It tells decision-makers both what the data shows and what it does not yet show.

usageFocus.description:
### Observation → Interpretation → Recommendation

- The data shows a 12% decline.

mainInput.title: 2. Main Input - Beyond the Price
mainInput.context: A technology company is negotiating a three-year outsourcing contract with a global service provider. The first two meetings focus almost entirely on price and reach an impasse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The buyer wants a 12% reduction. The provider says anything above 5% would make the contract unattractive.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: A new lead negotiator reframes the discussion. She asks both sides to rank the importance of five variables: price, payment timing, service levels, contract length, and access to future regional projects.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The pattern is revealing. The buyer cares most about predictable cost and service quality. The provider cares about contract length, early payment, and the possibility of future work.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator

dialogue.speaker: Narrator

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The agreement is more complex than either side's original position, but it works because the negotiation moves from distributive bargaining—who gives up how much—to value creation across issues with different priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The remaining skill is not merely finding tradeable variables. It is making concessions conditional, reciprocal, and explicit so that flexibility does not become one-sided surrender.

mainInput.title: 2. Main Input — Northstar Systems: A Company at a Crossroads
mainInput.context: Northstar Systems is a mid-sized business-software company. Revenue growth has slowed from 18% to 4%. A new AI-based competitor is winning smaller customers with a cheaper product. At the same time, Northstar's largest customers still value its reliability, support, and industry expertise.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The board faces several pressures.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: Investors want operating costs reduced by at least 10%. Employees are worried about automation after rumours of restructuring. The sales team wants lower prices to defend market share. Product leaders argue that cutting prices without simplifying the product will damage margins. The technology team wants a major AI investment. Customer support is already overloaded.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: There is also an opportunity: a regional partner proposes a joint expansion into two new markets. The investment would consume much of Northstar's available capital.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: No single move solves the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: A large AI programme may strengthen the product but delay cost savings. Aggressive layoffs may improve margins quickly but weaken support and implementation capability. Price cuts may protect volume but accelerate a race to the bottom. Expansion may create growth but increase complexity at the worst possible time.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The executive team must decide what Northstar will prioritise over the next 18 months—and, equally important, what it will not do.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: A credible strategy must connect diagnosis, choices, resource allocation, risk, and communication. It must also survive challenge from people who bear different consequences.
